ai.definition: Quantum computing is a type of computing that uses quantum bits or qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously due to the principles of superposition and entanglement. This allows quantum computers to perform complex calculations at speeds far beyond classical computers.
ai.howItWorks: Quantum computers leverage the properties of quantum mechanics such as superposition (where a qubit can be both 0 and 1 at the same time) and entanglement (where the state of one qubit is dependent on another, no matter the distance between them). These properties enable parallel processing capabilities that allow for solving certain problems much faster than classical computers.
ai.problemSolved: Challenges in fields requiring massive computational power such as cryptography, drug discovery, and optimization problems where classical computing methods are inefficient or impractical.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing quantum computers is highly complex due to the delicate nature of qubits. Current prototypes often use superconducting circuits or trapped ions, which require extremely low temperatures and isolation from external interference.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves creating stable qubits, implementing error correction codes, and developing algorithms that can run on these quantum systems. This is a highly specialized field requiring expertise in both hardware engineering and software development.
ai.costDrivers: High costs associated with maintaining ultra-cold temperatures (near absolute zero), the need for extremely low noise environments, and the complexity of building and scaling qubit arrays.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces significant challenges in scaling and practical application. The technology is expected to advance over the next decade as more robust error correction methods are developed and applications become clearer.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for quantum computing are still emerging, with concerns around data privacy, security, and potential misuse of advanced computational capabilities.
ai.risks: Technical risks include qubit instability, scalability issues, and the need for continuous cooling. Business risks involve high initial investment costs and uncertainty about long-term market demand and applications.
ai.profitability: Current profitability is limited due to the early stage of development and lack of widespread commercial applications. However, potential future markets in areas like pharmaceuticals, finance, and AI could drive significant economic impact if the technology matures.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments are expected to focus on improving qubit coherence times, increasing the number of qubits, and developing more efficient error correction methods. Additionally, there is ongoing research into new materials and architectures that could enhance performance.

glossary.def: A quantum bit, the basic unit of information in a quantum computer.
The principle that allows qubits to exist in multiple states simultaneously until measured.
A phenomenon where the state of one particle is dependent on another, even at great distances.
Methods used to detect and correct errors in quantum computations due to decoherence and other issues.

subsystems.name: Quantum processor
subsystems.role: holds and manipulates the qubits — the physical two-level systems that store the computation.
parts: qubit elements (superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, or photonic modes)

subsystems.name: Control and readout
subsystems.role: applies the precise pulses that execute gates and reads out the result.

subsystems.name: Cryogenics and vacuum
subsystems.role: keeps most qubit types cold enough to stay quantum for long enough.

subsystems.name: Error correction layer
subsystems.role: combines many imperfect physical qubits into a smaller number of reliable logical qubits.
parts: error-correcting codes such as the surface code

subsystems.name: Classical orchestration
subsystems.role: compiles algorithms into pulse sequences and calibrates the machine between runs.

subsystems.name: Networking and interconnects
subsystems.role: links separate modules so machines can grow beyond one chip or trap.

buildSteps.title: Pick a modality and design the chip
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether qubits will be superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms or photonic modes, then lay out the circuit or trap geometry and error-correction scheme.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the quantum hardware
buildSteps.detail: For superconducting chips, superconducting metal films are deposited on a silicon wafer and Josephson junctions are patterned by lithography; photonic chips use waveguides, splitters and squeezers instead.

buildSteps.title: Package and cool
buildSteps.detail: The chip is mounted in a shielded enclosure and wired with hundreds of coaxial or optical lines down through a dilution refrigerator to millikelvin temperatures, or held in an ultra-high-vacuum ion or atom trap.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the qubits
buildSteps.detail: Each qubit's frequency, gate timing and readout threshold are measured and tuned, since fabrication tolerances leave every device slightly different.

buildSteps.title: Run and benchmark gates and algorithms
buildSteps.detail: Single- and two-qubit gates are verified, then small circuits are run to measure fidelity, coherence time and cross-entropy or volume benchmarks.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate error correction
buildSteps.detail: Many physical qubits are grouped into a logical qubit via repeated syndrome measurements; the milestone is showing that adding more physical qubits lowers the logical error rate.

buildSteps.title: Scale and interconnect
buildSteps.detail: Qubit counts grow on a chip, and modules are linked with microwave or optical interconnects to reach the thousands of logical qubits real applications need.

buildSteps.title: Deploy through the cloud
buildSteps.detail: Users submit circuits over the internet to a hosted machine, with classical pre- and post-processing alongside the quantum run.

prerequisites.why: most qubits lose their quantum state if they are not held near absolute zero or in vacuum.
gate fidelities depend on controlling pulses to nanosecond precision and low phase noise.
gates and readout are still imperfect, so useful machines need many physical qubits per logical one — below-threshold correction has only recently been shown.

prerequisites.tech: Fabrication of quantum chips at scale
prerequisites.why: thousands of near-identical qubits with low defect rates need semiconductor-grade process control.
a machine able to run Shor's algorithm would break RSA and elliptic-curve encryption, so migration should happen before such a machine exists.

pathway.milestone: cloud-accessible processors with tens to hundreds of noisy physical qubits, and early demonstrations that error rates fall as qubit arrays grow
pathway.unlocks: hands-on experimentation and a real testbed for error-correction codes.
simulating molecules and materials beyond the reach of classical computers, where the first clear advantage is expected.

pathway.milestone: thousands of logical qubits with networked modules
pathway.unlocks: Fault-tolerant operation and useful chemistry, optimisation and machine-learning tasks.
Running Shor's algorithm against current public-key cryptography — the scenario the NIST post-quantum standards published in 2024 are meant to pre-empt.
